newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak president says referendum scuppers NATO bid.
newsitem.headline: Slovak president says referendum scuppers NATO bid.

text.p: Slovak President Michal Kovac said on Monday that the failure of a referendum seen as a test of democracy had ruined Slovakia's last chances of early membership of NATO and the EU.

Slovakia's widely boycotted weekend referendum was declared officially void on Monday and a member of the Central Referendum Committee denounced ballot papers distributed by the Interior Ministry as a "massive swindle".

"With great probability, this has ruined our last chance of being among the first contenders for membership in NATO and the European Union," Kovac said in a statement to the nation. "We are really facing international isolation."
Within hours, Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik, charged with persuading Western capitals that Slovakia was progressing towards integration with the EU and NATO, had tendered his resignation.

"Contemporary political events in Slovakia, especially the circumstances surrounding the referendum ... have to the greatest possible extent narrowed the scope for me as foreign minister to pursue the foreign policy priorities of our nation," Hamzik said in a statement.

Western diplomats told Reuters Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar had invited EU ambassadors accredited to Bratislava to meet him later on Monday when he was expected to present his view of the referendum.
The referendum had been billed as a last chance for Slovakia, which has come under fire from the West for lack of democracy, to revive its hopes of an invitation to join NATO.

Instead, the vote was turned into chaos by Prime Minister Meciar's long-running rivalry with Kovac, who wanted a question about presidential elections on the ballot and led the boycott when it was struck off at the last moment.
Meciar on Sunday had placed the blame for the referendum's failure on Kovac and the opposition.
"The biggest responsibility for the worsening situation of our country in the world...lies personally with...Meciar," Kovac said in the statement distributed to journalists.

"(Meciar's ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia) should seriously consider whether the departure of the premier and interior minister from political life would not bring considerable relief for our sorely tested land," he added.
The central referendum committee refused even to count the result, saying the small number of voters who went to the polls on Friday and Saturday wasted their time because the ballots were illegal.
Kovac and his supporters want future presidents elected directly, a change that might head off the ambitions of Meciar, who could inherit presidential powers if the choice remains with parliament.
Interior Minister Gustav Krajci removed the election question from the ballots at the last minute, claiming the Constitutional Court had declared it illegal.
The government tried to go ahead with the remaining ballot asking whether Slovaks want to join NATO. But many thousands of electors followed the president in refusing to take part.
"The referendum... was nullified," Referendum Committee vice-chairman Jozef Krumpolec told a news conference.

"The total number of eligible voters taking part in the vote was nil. The number of citizens who replied "Yes" and those who replied "No" cannot be assessed because no (valid) ballot papers were delivered."

Kovac expressed fears that Slovakia's association agreement with the EU could also be threatened following several expressions of concern both from the EU and the United States over foot-dragging on democratic reforms.

"There is grave concern abroad over the stability of democratic development in Slovakia which leads foreign politicians to the conclusion that Slovakia is becoming a problem of central Europe," Kovac said.
